Futures are pointing to a mixed start for the U.S. equity market.

That’s a lot of cheese

 

U.S. investors don’t talk much about the 2011 bear market. That’s because it never entered the record books—the unofficial threshold of a 20% decline in stocks only got hit on an intraday basis.

 

But the fears that helped send the market to the brink 15 years ago, Europe’s debt woes and U.S. bond market jitters, are back in the headlines. Instead of Greece and the other “PIIGS” being the sick men of Europe, this time it’s France—the continent’s biggest borrower. The country’s 10-year debt yields are a full percentage point more than the equivalent bonds from Germany, with which it shares a currency.

 

That doesn’t yet spook people who mainly invest in America with its AI wonder companies. For all its borrowing, France has a smaller stock market than Canada, Switzerland or even Taiwan, and isn’t home to many tech companies.

 

But then there’s a reason tiny Greece weighed on stocks globally—the prospect of a financial crisis that could spill beyond its borders, and Europe’s, too. 

 

Two things are different today: France would be a much tougher problem to solve with its €3.5 trillion in debt. And other sovereign spendthrifts, including Britain and the U.S., have meanwhile piled up a lot more liabilities.

 

America’s borrowing levels were in the headlines in 2011 mostly because the U.S. lost its triple-A credit rating from Standard & Poor’s that summer, not because bond yields were near multidecade highs the way they are today. 

 

As vexing as America’s fiscal picture seems, France is in worse shape. And its politics make Washington look like a bastion of bonhomie. Violent protests erupted in 2023 when President Emmanuel Macron bypassed parliament to gradually raise the retirement age to 64.

 

The far-right front-runner in next spring’s presidential election wants to lower it while her far-left challenger wants France’s central bank to just cancel the debt it holds. Pick your poison, but those pledges are adding billions of euros to France’s annual borrowing costs today.

 

They might be even higher if not for a potential backstop. In 2012, the then president of the European Central Bank created a precedent for a rescue with his “whatever it takes” pledge.

 

But the current mechanism for doing that requires France to enact strict spending rules. If they’re fudged, outright bond buying to pay for French social benefits could spill over to other European countries’ bond markets.

 

That would be a mess, and probably not a foreign debacle we only read about.

 

There’s no clear domestic trigger for when Americans have to worry about unsustainable budget math at home. It could well come from Europe.
